title: HEART Score vs Troponin-Alone: The Transatlantic Chest Pain Divide — 2026-08-13

sources.title: ACEP Clinical Policy: Suspected Non-ST-Elevation ACS
sources.why: ACEP's live Level B position: HEART <3 plus a single/serial troponin gives a 0-2% miss rate — the US anchor for 'calculate the score before you discharge.'

sources.title: NICE HTG552: High-sensitivity troponin tests for the early rule out of NSTEMI
sources.why: The listener's own national guidance: rule-out via single below-limit-of-detection or serial hs-cTn sampling, no mandated risk score anywhere in the pathway — the direct NHS counterpoint to ACEP.

sources.title: Risk Scores for Clinical Risk Stratification of ED Chest Pain (O'Rielly et al., CJC 2023)
sources.why: The evidence behind the NICE/ESC stance: once hs-cTn has ruled out MI, residual 30-day MACE risk is already so low that HEART 'may be of little additional value' — a systematic review directly undercutting ACEP's Level B recommendation.

sources.title: Clinical decision rules are ruining medicine - First10EM
sources.why: Morgenstern's methodological grenade: HEART-style derivation/validation studies overstate real-world discriminative value via spectrum bias and easy-case inclusion — reinforces the anti-CDR side with a citable mechanism, not just outcome data.

sources.title: 2025 ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI Guideline for Acute Coronary Syndromes
sources.why: Brand-new (2025) joint US guideline — ACEP co-authored — endorses clinical decision pathways generically (21-43% less unnecessary testing) but stops short of mandating HEART, proving the divide isn't even settled within US cardiology/EM itself.

sources.title: MDCalc Wars: HEART Score Vs. EDACS - REBEL EM
sources.why: June 2025 head-to-head: even doctors who accept a score should exist can't agree which one — grounds the debate in the practical 'what do I actually press on MDCalc' decision UK and US clinicians both face.

rationale: This stays a debate because the evidence has genuinely not converged: ACEP's live 2018 policy (reaffirmed in its 2025 joint guideline's refusal to mandate a score) gives HEART a Level B recommendation, while NICE — the listener's own national body — and the 2023 ESC guidelines build rule-out entirely around hs-troponin algorithms with no risk score at all, a structural philosophical split rather than a minor disagreement. A 2023 systematic review (O'Rielly) supplies the evidence engine for the biomarker-only camp, showing HEART adds little once hs-cTn has ruled out MI, while First10EM's methodological critique explains *why* HEART-style derivation studies might overstate real-world value in the first place. REBEL EM's 2025 HEART-vs-EDACS comparison keeps the debate practical rather than purely philosophical, forcing the hosts to argue not just "score or no score" but "if a score, which one." The mix of a UK national guideline, a US clinical policy, a systematic review, a FOAMed methodological takedown, and a head-to-head tool comparison gives both hosts real, current, citable ammunition on opposite sides — ideal for a UK EM doctor who lives inside the NICE pathway but constantly encounters US-trained HEART-first teaching.
case_vignette: A 54-year-old smoker presents at 02:00 with 40 minutes of central chest tightness that resolved before arrival, a normal ECG, and a first hs-troponin just below the assay's rule-out threshold. Following NICE, the treating registrar wants to discharge on the single below-limit-of-detection sample alone; the visiting US fellow insists on calculating a HEART score first, pointing out the patient's risk factors push him into a moderate-risk band despite the reassuring troponin. Whose protocol is actually safer for this patient walking out the door tonight — and whose is just extra paperwork?
